studies.title: By The Sky Of Towers
studies.meaning: Three oaths, and the third is deliberately unresolved: a witness and a witnessed, with neither identified. The classical commentaries offer many pairings and record them without choosing. What the oaths lead to is not a claim but a curse, pronounced on people described only by a place: the companions of the trench. Then the trench is named as fire, and the fire is given fuel, and the reader is left with an execution ground before being told a single thing about who was in it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah addresses a community under pressure and offers it an older case of the same thing. The commentators connect the trench to a persecution in southern Arabia in which believers were burnt for their faith, and the classical collections preserve a long report about a boy, a monk and a king that is told alongside it. The sources differ over the place and the period, and they record the differences.

keyTerms.note: The word for a fortified tower, applied to the great figures of stars. It occurs four times in the Quran, and the surah takes its name from it, so the chapter about a trench opens with towers.
A furrow or groove cut into the ground, from a root also used of the cheek. It occurs once in the Quran and describes the site by its shape, which is what makes the image so exact.

What a fire is fed with, as distinct from the fire itself. Naming it separately says the blaze was maintained rather than lit, which turns an execution into an operation someone had to keep supplying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Southern Arabia was not a distant place to a Meccan. The incense road ran through it, the great kingdoms there were within living memory of trading families, and news of what had happened in those cities travelled north with every caravan. A story about believers burnt in a ditch in the south was recent history rather than legend, and the audience for this surah were themselves under pressure at home.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is named after a word for towers and opens with it, then immediately describes a trench dug in the ground. Both words occur in the first four ayat, and the chapter's whole geography runs between them, from the constellations to a ditch. The word for the trench appears nowhere else in the Quran.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Swearing by the sky and by a promised day before naming a historical atrocity places that atrocity inside a much longer measurement. The curse is pronounced in the past tense on people who at the time appeared to have won completely. That is the passage's claim: the verdict on an event is not the verdict its participants recorded, and the oaths establish who is keeping the other record.

crossReferences.why: Also speaks of towers set in the sky, adorned for those who look at them.
Lists towns given respite and then seized, so that the outcome came long after the appearance of success.
Recalls earlier peoples who plotted against their messengers, and how the seizure eventually fell.

studies.applyIt: Read the first five ayat of this surah once and stop at the fourth, before any explanation arrives. Notice that you have been given a verdict on people you have not yet met. Sit with the order for a moment. The surah judges before it describes, and reading it in that order once is the only way to feel what it is doing.

studies.title: They Sat And Watched
studies.meaning: The detail that carries the passage is posture. They were sitting at the edge of the fire, and they were witnesses to what was being done. Nothing describes their cruelty; the verb given them is watching. Then the motive is stated by elimination. They held nothing against these people except that they believed in God, and the two names attached to God at that point are the Mighty and the Praiseworthy. The sentence names the whole grievance and finds it empty in the same clause.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and addressed to a community facing pressure of its own. The commentators read the passage as consolation offered by precedent rather than by promise: it does not say the believers in the trench were rescued. What is emphasised instead is the exactness of the record, which mattered to an audience whose own sufferings were public, small in scale, and beneath the notice of the city.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the participle for one who is sitting. It describes them at rest while the thing is done, which is the detail the passage chooses over any description of the violence itself.
Those present at an event and able to testify to it. The same root supplies the oath in the third ayah and the name for God at the end of this passage, so the word runs through the whole opening.
To find fault with something and take revenge for it. The verb assumes a grievance, and the sentence then supplies one that is not a grievance at all, which is where the irony sits.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public punishment was theatre. Executions and floggings were held where people could gather, and attendance was part of how a ruler made a point, so the crowd was not incidental to the event but a component of it. Anyone in Mecca hearing about men seated at the edge of a fire would have pictured a familiar arrangement: benches, an audience, and a proceeding conducted in good order.
studies.didYouKnow: One root runs through the first nine ayat of this surah and appears four times: in the oath by a witness and a witnessed, in the description of these men as onlookers, and in the closing statement that God is witness over everything. The persecutors are given the same word as the third oath, and then the word is taken from them and given to God.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Stating the grievance and finding it to be nothing but belief exposes persecution as motiveless in the strict sense: there is no injury to point at. The names chosen for God in that same line are the Mighty and the Praiseworthy, which answers the two things the persecutors had, power and public approval. Both are quietly transferred, and the transfer is made inside the sentence describing the crime.

crossReferences.why: Records the same accusation in another persecution, that they were held against only for believing.
Uses the same verb to ask whether anything is held against them except that they believed in God.
Says people are not left untested on their claim of belief, and that those before them were tested too.

studies.applyIt: Think about the last time you watched something unfair happen and stayed seated. Not a crime, just a room where someone was being humiliated. The passage does not describe those who lit the fire. It describes those who sat and observed. Recall one such moment and give it a plain name today, without excusing it.

studies.title: Unless They Turn Back
studies.meaning: One line settles the case of the persecutors, and it contains a condition that changes everything about it. Those who put the believing men and the believing women to the fire and then did not turn back have two punishments named for them. The clause about turning back is not an aside. It means that repentance was on the table for people who had burnt others alive, and the sentence is constructed so that only their refusal, not their crime, closes the door. Both groups of victims are named separately.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is addressing a community whose own members were being pressured, some of them severely, and this ayah tells them what the position of their persecutors actually is. The commentators note that the door held open here is the same door held open across the Meccan surahs to the leadership of the city. No occasion is reported for the ayah, which speaks of the earlier persecution rather than a current one.

keyTerms.note: The root originally means to assay gold by putting it in fire, and from there to test, tempt and persecute. In a passage about a burning trench the literal sense of the metaphor is directly in view.
The verb is simply to return, used of coming back to a place. Repentance in Arabic is not primarily remorse but reversal of direction, which is why the condition can be stated so briefly.
The noun for a fire that consumes, distinct from the general word for fire. Its use here answers the trench exactly, so the punishment named is the one they administered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gold and silver were assayed by fire, and the metalworkers of the trading towns did it as routine work: heat the sample, see what comes out, price it accordingly. The verb used in this ayah for what was done to the believers is that verb. An audience that bought and sold precious metal would have heard the technical sense underneath the terrible one.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names believing men and believing women separately rather than using a single plural for both, which the Quran does deliberately in a small number of places. It also uses, for what was done to them, the verb that literally means to test metal in fire, so the vocabulary of the crime and the vocabulary of assaying are the same word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing a conditional clause inside a sentence of condemnation is the whole theological content of the line. Nothing is said about the crime being too great, and no exception is made for the scale of it. What determines the outcome is a direction of travel afterwards. That sets an outer boundary on how far mercy is described as reaching, and the boundary is drawn by the offender rather than by the offence.

crossReferences.why: Tells those who went to excess against themselves not to despair of God's mercy, which forgives all sins.
Lists the gravest wrongs and then says that whoever turns back and works good has his evil exchanged.
States that whoever turns back after wrongdoing and sets things right will be turned toward in return.

studies.applyIt: Think of a person you have decided is past the point of change, and notice that this ayah does not make that decision about people who burnt believers in a ditch. You do not have to reopen anything with them. Just withdraw the verdict privately, today, and see how much of your feeling about them was resting on it.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: The Forgiving, The Loving
studies.meaning: The other side of the case is given in one ayah and called the great triumph, and then the surah turns entirely to God. The seizing of your Lord is severe. He originates and He brings back. And He is the Forgiving, the Loving. Four descriptions in four short lines, and they do not settle into a single tone: the harshest statement in the surah and the tenderest name in it stand two lines apart, with the making and remaking of everything between them, and nothing reconciles them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just described a persecution and its two outcomes, and the commentators read this run of divine descriptions as the ground of both, given without separating them into a list of severity and a list of mercy. No occasion is reported. For a community with no protection in the city, the assertion that the grip of their Lord is severe was consolation rather than warning.

keyTerms.note: To take hold of someone violently with the hand, the word for a grip that cannot be broken. It describes a physical action rather than a judicial one, which is why the ayah reads as it does.
From a root for warm attachment, the word used of affection between people. It occurs twice in the Quran, and the other place has an earlier prophet using it while calling his people to turn back.
Nobility joined with generosity, said in Arabic of a person whose rank and whose openhandedness are the same thing. The surah uses this word twice, here and in its final lines.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A grip was the currency of Arabian justice. There were no police and no gaol; a wrong was settled when someone with the strength to do so laid hands on the offender, which meant that having no strong clan behind you left you with no remedy at all. The believers being described had exactly that problem, and the ayah answers it in the vocabulary of a hand closing on someone.
studies.didYouKnow: The name meaning the Loving occurs twice in the whole Quran. Here it stands two ayat after the statement that the grip of your Lord is severe, and the other occurrence is spoken by an earlier prophet at the end of a call to repentance, paired there with the name of mercy. Both times the word appears in the middle of a warning rather than apart from one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places severity and love in the same short breath and does not resolve the tension, which is deliberate. A God described only as severe would be a threat and a God described only as loving would be an indulgence, and neither would explain the case just narrated, in which people were burnt and their killers were offered a way back. The list here is the explanation, and it is left as a list.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other use of the name the Loving, at the close of a call to seek forgiveness.
Uses the same word for the seizing, there of a single great seizure on a named day.
Says that God will appoint affection for those who believe and do good, from the same root as the name here.

studies.applyIt: Say the two lines to yourself in the order the surah gives them: the grip is severe, and He is the Forgiving, the Loving. Most people carry one of those and not the other, and can tell you within a second which. Notice which one you had to reach for, and leave it at the noticing.

studies.title: Two Armies Already Gone
studies.meaning: A question is put to the listener in the form the Quran uses when the answer is meant to be yes. Has the account of the armies reached you. Two are named and no story is told about either, because the outcome is the only part being cited. Then the reply to the whole surah's argument: those who deny are simply in a state of denial. And a last clause places God behind them, using a word for something that surrounds a thing on every side while remaining out of view.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Pharaoh and Thamud are the two examples the Quran returns to most often for organised power that ended, one foreign and remembered from scripture, the other Arabian and marked by ruins on the trade road north that Meccan caravans passed. Naming the pair together assumes the audience knew both. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a body of troops. It names both parties by their organised strength rather than by belief, which fits a passage whose subject is the failure of power rather than the failure of an argument.
A verbal noun rather than a verb, so denial is described as a condition they are inside rather than an act they perform. The Arabic literally places them in it, as one might be in a place.
From a root about a wall going round something. It is used of a besieging force and of knowledge that leaves nothing outside it, and both senses work in a passage about armies.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The ruins of Thamud stood on the caravan route between Mecca and Syria, and traders passed them twice a year. Rock-cut facades in a valley, and no people. Pharaoh's Egypt was equally real to them through the grain trade and the accounts of travellers. Both examples in this ayah could be reached from Mecca, and men in the audience had stood in one of the two places.
studies.didYouKnow: The question opening this passage uses a formula the Quran employs six times, always to introduce something the listener has already heard. Two of those six occurrences are in the surahs immediately around this one, and one opens the surah that comes three chapters later, so the same three-word phrase recurs three times in a short stretch of the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming two powers and telling neither story makes the point that the outcome is the argument. Nothing is offered about why they fell, only that the account exists. Then denial is described as a place rather than an act, and God as surrounding them from behind, which reverses the usual picture of a besieged people looking outward. The ones who appear to hold the ground are the ones enclosed.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same kind of vanished powers, ending with the statement that your Lord is on the lookout.
Calls the opposition a defeated host and names the earlier peoples, including Thamud and Pharaoh.
Ends a surah with the same word, saying that God encompasses everything, after a passage about doubt.

studies.applyIt: Look up a photograph of the rock-cut tombs of Thamud, which takes a minute. The audience for this ayah had seen them from a camel's back on the way to Syria. Having the image in mind changes what the two names in this passage do, from a list into two places you could visit.

studies.title: In A Guarded Tablet
studies.meaning: The surah ends with a correction and a location. Against everything just said about denial stands what this actually is: a glorious recitation, in a preserved tablet. The adjective given to it is the one given four ayat earlier to the Throne, so the same word describes the seat of authority and the text. And the last word of the chapter is a passive participle: guarded. After a surah about believers who could not be protected, the closing note is about something that is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The chapter has moved from an atrocity nobody prevented to a text nobody can reach, and the commentators read the closing pair as the surah's answer rather than as an appendix. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The community hearing them had no written copy of what they were memorising, which makes the image of a kept tablet a claim about somewhere other than Mecca.

keyTerms.note: Rank and openhandedness in one word. The surah applies it to the Throne and then to the recitation, so the same quality is attributed to the seat of authority and to the words that come from it.
A plain wooden or stone board of the kind used for writing lessons and notices. The word is deliberately ordinary, and the phrase it forms here occurs nowhere else in the Quran.
A passive participle from the verb to keep and protect, the same root as the word for one who has memorised the Quran. Preservation and memorisation are one idea in Arabic, not two.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A tablet was a schoolroom object. Children learning letters wrote on a flat board and washed it clean to write again, and notices were posted on boards where people gathered. The word carried no grandeur at all. Setting the most ordinary writing surface in the language beside the word for a throne is the surah's last move, and the plainness of it is the point.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the preserved tablet occurs once in the Quran and only here. The adjective describing the recitation in the line before it is used twice in this same surah, once of the Throne, and elsewhere in the Book it opens another chapter as a description of the Quran itself. The surah's two grandest words are attached to a text and a board.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Locating the recitation outside the reach of anyone who could destroy it answers the whole surah. Believers in a trench could be killed and their killers could sit and watch. What is asserted at the close is not that such things are prevented but that the record and the message are not among the things that can be lost. That is a narrower claim than protection, and it is the one the chapter actually makes.

crossReferences.why: Opens another surah by swearing by the glorious Quran, using the identical adjective for it.
States that the reminder was sent down and that it is guarded, using the same root as this ayah.
Places the recitation in a hidden book and calls it a sending down from the Lord of the worlds.

studies.applyIt: Memorise two ayat you do not yet know, and choose short ones. The word this surah ends on, for something preserved, is the same word used for a person who carries the Quran in memory. Twenty minutes puts you inside the image rather than beside it, which is a different way of reading the last line of this chapter.
